960.title: Aryadeva
960.hook: Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on
960.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Aryadeva's Four Hundred verses are studied alongside Nagarjuna's works in the Madhyamaka curriculum, and teachers explain its verse on the order of teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suhrllekha, Nagarjuna's letter of advice to a royal friend: honor it like a Buddha carved from plain wood. What did your own letter say? Day nine hundred sixty.

A great teacher is only half of a lineage. The other half is the person who listens closely enough to carry it after the teacher is gone. Nagarjuna had such a student. His name was Aryadeva, and tradition remembers him less for inventing a new idea than for taking his teacher's middle way out into the world and testing it. In debate halls, against rival schools, and in verses of his own. Today, the one who carried it on.
screen: `HALF OF A LINEAGE.` → `ARYADEVA, THE STUDENT.` → `TAKING THE MIDDLE WAY OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the eye. Tradition also calls him Kanadeva, and explains the name as the one-eyed deva, and tells a legend to account for it. Someone admired one of his eyes, so he took it out and gave it away, to show that the body is not worth clinging to. It is a legend, and it is told to make a point about letting go. Second, his book. Aryadeva wrote a work called the Four Hundred, a collection of verses that takes Nagarjuna's emptiness and puts it to work against clinging: to permanence, to the body, to pleasure, to the self. Third, a teacher's order. One verse in it lays out an order. First turn a student away from harmful actions. Then, in the middle, away from the idea of a solid self. And last, away from every view at all. Even emptiness is not a place to cling. That is a teacher thinking about how a student actually grows: one step, then the next. Fourth, a hard ending. A Chinese account of his life says a follower of a rival he had defeated in debate attacked him with a knife. As he lay dying, Aryadeva told his own students not to chase the man, and spoke of the attacker with compassion. In that telling, the last thing he taught was the teaching itself, lived. A student who carried it to the end.
screen: `KANADEVA, THE ONE-EYED.` · `THE FOUR HUNDRED VERSES.` · `HARM, THEN SELF, THEN ALL VIEWS.` · `DON'T CHASE HIM.` · then, large: `THE STUDENT CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from a student's student. Bring to mind one thing a teacher showed you, a way of cooking, of fixing something, of calming down. Settle, and breathe. Ask how you do it now. What did you keep exactly as you were shown? What did you test for yourself, and change? Aryadeva took his teacher's way and tried it out in the world. Notice where you have done the same. Then rest with it. The bell holds the time.
Aryadeva. Nagarjuna's student, who wrote the Four Hundred verses and, in a Chinese account, forgave the man who struck him down. Today's word.
Your line: the student carries it. Today, pass on one small thing someone taught you, and if you can, say who taught it. Day nine hundred sixty.

Aryadeva's verse says to cling to emptiness at the end

options: catch him and bring him to justice.
let him go, and hold him with compassion.
forget him and debate his teacher again.
fork.reveal: in the Chinese account, Aryadeva told his students not to chase the man, and spoke of him with compassion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a minor name in Nagarjuna's shadow.
what it means: the student who carried the middle way into debate and verse, and in one account forgave the man who attacked him.
what a scholar hears: the Four Hundred, and its verse on the order of teaching: first turn from harm, then from a self, then from all views.

961.title: Asanga and the dog
961.hook: after years of failure, Asanga tends a wounded dog and Maitreya appears (a legend)
961.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist teachers tell the story of Asanga and the dog when teaching great compassion, and Asanga is honored in Tibetan tradition as a founder of the lineage of vast activity received from Maitreya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aryadeva, Nagarjuna's student. Your line was the student carries it. What did you pass on, and did you say who taught you? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A monk sits alone in a cave on a mountain. His name is Asanga, and he has one wish: to see Maitreya, the Buddha who is to come, face to face, and learn from him. He meditates for years. Nothing. He gives up and walks down the mountain, sees something that shames him into trying again, and climbs back up. Years more. Nothing. This happens again and again. At last, Tibetan tellers say, he leaves for good. On the road down, a dog is lying in the dust. Today, Maitreya.
screen: `A CAVE, AND ONE WISH.` → `YEARS, AND NOTHING.` → `A DOG IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the failures. In the telling, each time Asanga quits, he meets a small lesson in patience. A man rubbing an iron bar with a soft cloth, to make a needle. Drops of water that have worn a hollow into stone. Each one sends him back up the mountain. Each time, still nothing. Second, the dog. On his final walk down he finds the dog, its back half an open wound, crawling with maggots. And something in him breaks open. He wants to help the dog, but he does not want to kill the maggots either. So he cuts flesh from his own thigh to give them somewhere to go. Then, so as not to crush them with his fingers, he closes his eyes and bends down to lift them away with his tongue. Third, the eyes open. His tongue touches the ground. The dog is gone. Maitreya stands there, shining. Asanga, in tears, asks why he never came in all those years. And Maitreya answers that he was always there. What hid him was Asanga's own mind, until great compassion cleared it. Fourth, the proof. To show it, the story says, Asanga carries Maitreya on his shoulder into the town. Almost no one sees anything. One old woman sees only a dog. This is a legend, and Tibetan teachers tell it as one, with a point. Tradition goes on to credit Asanga with teachings received from Maitreya, which became the ground of the school we meet in two days. But the story's own lesson is simpler. It was not effort alone that let him see. Compassion opened his eyes.
screen: `A NEEDLE FROM AN IRON BAR.` · `HIS OWN FLESH FOR THE MAGGOTS.` · `I WAS ALWAYS HERE.` · `ONE OLD WOMAN SEES A DOG.` · then, large: `COMPASSION OPENED HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tend one hurting thing. It can be small. A wilted plant that needs water. A friend who has gone quiet. A sore muscle in your own back. Settle, and breathe. Bring it to mind, or go to it if it's near. Give it plain attention first, the way Asanga finally looked at the dog. Then decide on one gentle thing you can do for it, today. Rest with that intention. The bell holds the time.
Maitreya. The Buddha who is to come, whom Asanga saw at last in the place of a wounded dog he had tended. Today's word.
Your line: compassion opened his eyes. Today, when something or someone looks like a nuisance in the road, slow down once and look again. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Vasubandhu
962.hook: Asanga's brother, who wrote a great summary of the Abhidharma, then turned to "mind only"
962.howItsDone: Vasubandhu's Treasury of Abhidharma is studied in Tibetan monastic colleges and in East Asian Buddhist scholarship, and his later verse works are core texts of the Yogacara school.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asanga and the dog, and Maitreya where the dog had been. Your line was compassion opened his eyes. What hurting thing did you tend? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Asanga had a younger brother. He was brilliant, sharp in debate, and, at first, not impressed by his older brother's new Mahayana teachings at all. In fact, the old account says, he mocked them. His name was Vasubandhu, and before he was done he would write a great handbook of Buddhist thought, and then become a voice for the very teaching he had laughed at. A clever person who changed his mind in public. Today, Vasubandhu.
screen: `ASANGA'S YOUNGER BROTHER.` → `HE MOCKED THE NEW TEACHING.` → `THEN HE CHANGED HIS MIND.`

segments.voice: First, the treasury. Vasubandhu studied the Abhidharma, the careful lists that break experience into its smallest parts: moments of mind, kinds of feeling, causes and conditions. He gathered it into verses with his own commentary, the Abhidharmakosha, the Treasury of Abhidharma. Here and there in the commentary he quietly disagrees with the school he is summarizing. Even his handbook argues. Second, the turn. The Life of Vasubandhu, an old account kept in Chinese, tells it this way. Asanga, worried for his brother, sent word that he was ill. Vasubandhu came. That night he heard a Mahayana sutra being recited, and something in it reached him. He saw that he had been wrong, and he was so ashamed of the words he had spoken against it that he wanted to cut out his own tongue. Third, the answer. Asanga told him no. The tongue that had spoken against the teaching could now speak for it. Use it differently. So Vasubandhu did. Fourth, what he wrote next. He turned to the Mahayana, and wrote short, dense verses and commentaries on how the mind shapes what it sees, the teaching called mind only, which we open tomorrow. Some later writers have wondered whether two different men named Vasubandhu lie behind all these books. Tradition remembers one. Either way, the story's lesson stays the same. He did not hide his old self. He changed his mind, and put the same sharp tongue to new work.
screen: `THE TREASURY OF ABHIDHARMA.` · `A SUTRA HEARD AT NIGHT.` · `USE THE TONGUE DIFFERENTLY.` · `ON TO MIND ONLY.` · then, large: `HE CHANGED HIS MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use the tongue differently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you once said against a person, a place or an idea, and later saw differently. No need to cut anything out. Asanga's answer was to use the same voice for something better. So find one fair, true thing you could say now in its favor. Say it silently, once, and notice how it sits in the mouth. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Vasubandhu. Asanga's brother, who wrote the Treasury of Abhidharma, mocked the Mahayana, then turned to it and wrote on mind only. Today's word.
Your line: he changed his mind. Today, if you find you were wrong about something, say so out loud to one person, and let it be simple. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Mind only
963.hook: the Yogacara school: how the mind shapes the world it sees
963.howItsDone: Yogacara texts are studied in Tibetan monastic curricula and in East Asian Buddhism, where the Faxiang school carried them, and their account of mind and seeds shapes how teachers in those traditions explain meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vasubandhu, who mocked the Mahayana and then wrote for it. Your line was he changed his mind. Which opinion of yours shifted? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A dream can hold a street, a house, a stranger who speaks, even a fear that makes the heart race. While it lasts, all of it seems solid and outside. Then comes waking, and it was all made by the mind. Vasubandhu, the brother who changed his mind, builds one of his short verse works around exactly this kind of example. He asks: what if waking life is shaped by the mind far more than it seems? Today, the school that asked it.
screen: `A DREAM FEELS SOLID.` → `THEN YOU WAKE.` → `WHAT IF WAKING IS SHAPED TOO?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Yogacara as the practice of yoga, the path of meditators. The school grew from the teachings tradition credits to Asanga and Maitreya, and from Vasubandhu's verses. Its other name is mind only. Second, the dream. In his Twenty Verses, Vasubandhu argues that, as in a dream, places and times and other beings can appear vividly with nothing outside the mind behind them. He adds a stranger picture. Where people see a river of water, he says, hungry ghosts see a river of pus. Same river, different minds, different worlds. Third, the storehouse. Yogacara teachers describe a deep layer of mind, the storehouse consciousness, where every action leaves a seed. When a seed ripens, it shapes how the next moment looks. So the anger of yesterday tints what you see today. Fourth, how to read it. Some readers, in India, Tibet and today, take Yogacara to say there is no world outside the mind at all. Others say it is describing experience: we never meet the world raw, only as our minds have shaped it, and that is what practice works on. Madhyamaka teachers in Tibet debated Yogacara closely, and Tibetan monastic colleges still study both schools. A much older line, from the Dhammapada in Max Müller's translation, points in a similar direction: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Yogacara takes that thought in its own direction. The mind does not just react to the world. It colors it.
screen: `YOGACARA: THE PATH OF MEDITATORS.` · `A RIVER OF WATER, A RIVER OF PUS.` · `SEEDS IN THE STOREHOUSE.` · `NO WORLD, OR NO RAW WORLD?` · then, large: `THE MIND COLORS IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your mind coloring one thing. Pick something in front of you, or a person you'll see today. Settle, and breathe. First, notice the color your mind already gives it. Pleasant, annoying, boring, dear. Now ask where that color came from. A memory, a mood, a habit. You don't have to remove it. Just see it as a color laid on top, and look at the thing underneath for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Yogacara. The path of meditators, also called mind only: the school of Asanga and Vasubandhu that looks at how the mind shapes the world it sees. Today's word.
Your line: the mind colors it. Today, when something irritates you, ask once whether the irritation is in the thing, or in the color you brought to it. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

pairs: the practice of yoga, the meditators' path
solid while it lasts, made by the mind

a river of pus.

fork.reveal: same river, different minds, different worlds. Vasubandhu uses it to show how the mind shapes what it meets.

trapdoor: what you thought: mind only means nothing is real.

964.title: Buddhist logic
964.hook: Dignaga and Dharmakirti: how we know what we know
964.howItsDone: In Tibetan monasteries, students train in debate built on Dignaga and Dharmakirti's logic, standing and clapping as they challenge a seated opponent, and Dharmakirti's works are a core part of the curriculum.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yogacara, the school of mind only. Your line was the mind colors it. What color did you catch your mind laying on something? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

Smoke is rising over a hill. Nobody can see a flame from here. And yet anyone watching would say, without a second thought, there's a fire up there. How do they know? They didn't see it. They worked it out. That small, ordinary step, from smoke to fire, became the standard example in a long Indian argument about knowing itself, and Buddhist teachers took part in it. If the mind colors everything, as yesterday's teachers said, then how can anyone trust what they know? Today, Buddhist logic.
screen: `SMOKE OVER A HILL.` → `NO FLAME IN SIGHT.` → `HOW DO WE KNOW?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Indian thinkers of different schools argued over pramana, the valid ways of knowing: what counts as real evidence? Buddhist teachers joined the argument, because the path depends on seeing things as they are, not as we wish. Second, Dignaga. Dignaga, a Buddhist teacher in the line of Vasubandhu, cut the list down. In his Compendium on Valid Knowledge, he holds that there are two ways of knowing. Perception: the bare meeting with what is in front of you, before words get attached. And inference: reasoning from a sign to what it points to, like smoke to fire. Everything else, he argued, either reduces to these or is not reliable knowing. Third, Dharmakirti. A later teacher, Dharmakirti, took Dignaga's work further and sharpened the rules of a good inference. The sign has to really belong to the thing. Smoke shows fire only because smoke cannot come without fire. A sign that only sometimes goes with a thing proves nothing. Fourth, why it matters off the page. These teachers were not doing logic for its own sake. They wanted a way to tell real knowing from mere opinion. A verse that later Buddhist writers quote, attributed to the Buddha, asks people to test his words the way a goldsmith tests gold, rather than take them on trust. Their work traveled to Tibet, where monks still practice debate, clapping to drive home each point, in a tradition built on these thinkers. The question they ask is simple enough for any kitchen table. How do you know?
screen: `PRAMANA: WHAT COUNTS AS KNOWING?` · `DIGNAGA: PERCEPTION AND INFERENCE.` · `DHARMAKIRTI: THE SIGN MUST BELONG.` · `TEST IT LIKE GOLD.` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU KNOW?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check how you know one thing. Choose a belief you're fairly sure of today. That a friend is upset with you. That the meeting will go badly. That you left the stove on. Settle, and breathe. Ask: did I perceive this, directly? Or did I infer it from a sign? If it's a sign, does the sign really belong to the thing, like smoke to fire, or only sometimes? Hold the answer gently, without needing to fix anything. The bell holds the time.
Buddhist logic. The tradition of Dignaga and Dharmakirti: two ways of knowing, perception and inference, and careful rules for telling a good sign from a bad one. Today's word.
Your line: how do you know. Today, before you pass on one piece of news or one judgment about someone, ask that question once, quietly. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

reasoning from a sign, like smoke to fire
sharpened the rules of a good sign

trapdoor: what you thought: logic is cold, and has little to do with a spiritual path.

965.title: Buddhaghosa
965.hook: the scholar whose Path of Purification maps the Theravada path
965.howItsDone: Theravada monks and meditation teachers study the Visuddhimagga as a guide to practice, and its account of virtue, concentration and wisdom shapes how the path is taught in Theravada monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhist logic, smoke and fire, Dignaga and Dharmakirti. Your line was how do you know. What did you catch yourself inferring? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

A scholar from India arrives at the Great Monastery in Sri Lanka. He wants to study the old commentaries kept there, in the island's own language, and put them into Pali. The elders are careful. Before handing over their treasures, they set him a test. They give him a few lines from the Buddha's own words and say, in effect: show us what you understand. His answer, the chronicle says, became a book. His name was Buddhaghosa. Today, the man and his map.
screen: `A SCHOLAR ARRIVES IN SRI LANKA.` → `THE ELDERS SET A TEST.` → `THE ANSWER BECOMES A BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In the Samyutta Nikaya, a deity asks the Buddha a riddle. There is a tangle inside and a tangle outside; people are caught in a tangle; who can untangle it? The Buddha answers: a wise person, standing firm in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom, can untangle the tangle. Those are the lines the elders gave. Second, the book. Buddhaghosa's answer was the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification. It takes the three things in the Buddha's reply, virtue, the mind trained in concentration, and wisdom, and builds the whole book around them, in that order. Third, the map. Inside, it lays out the path in practical detail: how to keep precepts, how to choose a meditation subject that suits your temperament, how concentration deepens, and what insight sees. It reads like a guide to the territory. Fourth, a legend with a wink. The chronicle says that when Buddhaghosa finished, the gods hid the book to test him, and he wrote it again. Hidden again, he wrote a third time. Then the first two reappeared, and when the elders read the three copies side by side, they matched, word for word. Tellers enjoy the story for what it says about him: he did not need the book to know the path. He had walked it before he mapped it.
screen: `A TANGLE INSIDE, A TANGLE OUTSIDE.` · `VIRTUE, CONCENTRATION, WISDOM.` · `A GUIDE TO THE TERRITORY.` · `THREE COPIES, WORD FOR WORD.` · then, large: `THE PATH MAPPED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one map. It can be a real one, a map of your town, or the map Buddhaghosa used: virtue, concentration, wisdom. Settle, and breathe. If you take his, ask gently where you are on it today. Is it a day for keeping one promise to yourself? For steadying the mind? For seeing something clearly? There's no grade here. Just find where you're standing, and rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Buddhaghosa. The scholar whose Path of Purification maps the way through virtue, concentration and wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: the path mapped. Today, when you feel tangled, name which of the three would help most right now: virtue, a steadier mind, or clearer seeing. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

the three things in the Buddha's answer to the tangle riddle.

966.title: The lazy monk
966.hook: a legend: Shantideva, thought lazy, is asked to recite, and recites a masterpiece
966.howItsDone: Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva is studied and recited in Tibetan Buddhism, and teachers tell the legend of his recitation at Nalanda when introducing the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhaghosa and his Path of Purification: virtue, concentration, wisdom. Your line was the path mapped. Where were you standing on the map? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A busy house can have one person who never seems to do anything. At the great monastery of Nalanda, the legend says, that person was a young monk named Shantideva. The others saw him eat, sleep and wander, and never study. Tradition says they gave him a teasing nickname for it. So they hatched a plan to embarrass him into leaving. They would invite him to give a public recitation, in front of everyone, and let him fail. Today, Shantideva.
screen: `A MONK WHO SEEMS TO DO NOTHING.` → `A PLAN TO EMBARRASS HIM.` → `A PUBLIC RECITATION.`

segments.voice: First, the trap. In the Tibetan telling, the monks set up a high teaching seat, some say on purpose without steps, and gathered a crowd to watch. Shantideva arrived, settled onto the seat without trouble, and asked a calm question. Shall I recite something old, or something new? Second, the surprise. They asked for something new, expecting nothing. And he began to recite the Bodhicharyavatara, the Way of the Bodhisattva: verses on the joy of the awakening mind, on patience, on effort, on meditation, on wisdom. The crowd went quiet. The lazy one spoke, and what came out was a masterpiece. Third, the vanishing. The legend says that when he reached the chapter on wisdom, at the verse where neither something nor nothing remains before the mind, he rose into the air and disappeared from sight, while his voice went on reciting. His work was gathered afterward from those who had heard it. Fourth, what the legend teaches. Nobody knew what was going on inside him. Quiet is not the same as empty. And that fits the week behind us. Aryadeva, the student who carried it. Asanga, whose eyes compassion opened. Vasubandhu, who changed his mind. Yogacara and the mind that colors everything. Logic asking how you know. Buddhaghosa's map. And now a monk everyone had judged, wrongly. Tomorrow we open one of his teachings.
